T0A01: 12 V is too low to shock you through skin. The danger is a short: huge current, which means burns, fire, even an explosion.
T0A02: All three are true: current through the body heats tissue, disrupts cell function, and makes muscles contract involuntarily.
T0A03: In US AC wiring, black = hot, white = neutral, green or bare = ground.
T0A04: A fuse removes power when there's an overload. It protects the wiring and gear, not you from shock.
T0A05: A bigger fuse lets too much current flow before it blows, so the wires can overheat and start a fire.
T0A06: All of these: three-wire cords, a common safety ground, and discharging high-voltage capacitors before working inside.
T0A07: Lightning arresters go on a grounded entry panel, where feed lines come into the building.
T0A08: A fuse or breaker goes in series with the hot wire only. Never the neutral.
T0A09: Bond all ground rods together with heavy wire or strap, so everything is at the same potential.
T0A10: Charging or discharging an unprotected battery too fast makes it overheat or out-gas (vent dangerous gas).
T0A11: Filter capacitors can hold a dangerous charge after the supply is switched off.
T0A12: Use a voltmeter and leads rated for the voltage you're measuring.
T0B01: Lightning wants a short, straight path. Keep ground connections short and direct, with no loops or sharp bends.
T0B02: All of these: training, staying tied off at all times, and an approved climbing harness.
T0B03: Never climb without a helper or observer.
T0B04: When putting up a tower, look for overhead power lines and stay well clear of them.
T0B05: A safety wire through a turnbuckle keeps vibration from unscrewing it.
T0B06: Place an antenna so that if it falls, no part can come within 10 feet of a power line.
T0B07: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it's fully retracted or has mechanical safety locks installed.
T0B08: Tower ground: a separate 8-foot ground rod at each leg, bonded to the tower and to each other.
T0B09: An antenna on a utility pole could touch high-voltage lines.
T0B10: Lightning grounding conductors: avoid sharp bends.
T0B11: Grounding requirements come from local electrical codes, not the FCC.
T0C01: Radio waves are non-ionizing radiation: not enough energy to break chemical bonds.
T0C02: Exposure limits are strictest from 30 to 300 MHz, where the body absorbs RF most. Of the choices, 50 MHz is in that range.
T0C03: Half the duty cycle = half the average exposure, so the allowed power density doubles (increases by a factor of 2).
T0C04: All of these affect exposure: frequency and power, distance, and the antenna's pattern.
T0C05: The body absorbs more RF at some frequencies than others, so the limits vary with frequency.
T0C06: All of these are acceptable: calculation from OET Bulletin 65, computer modeling, or calibrated field measurement.
T0C07: Touching an antenna while it transmits can give you an RF burn.
T0C08: To reduce exposure, move the antennas, since that's where the RF radiates from. Moving the transmitter doesn't help.
T0C09: Re-evaluate RF exposure whenever you change anything in the transmitter or antenna system.
T0C10: Duty cycle changes the average exposure, which is what the limits are based on.
T0C11: Duty cycle = the percentage of time the transmitter is actually transmitting.
T0C12: RF doesn't have enough energy to cause chemical changes or damage DNA. That's what makes it non-ionizing.
T0C13: The station licensee is responsible for keeping everyone under the RF exposure limits.
